coverage.category: 1. Household employers: domestic workers, live-in carers, nannies
coverage.found: Domestic employers must register with Social Security Commission (SSC; General Regulations 1995, separate form for domestic employers, employee registration within 30 days) and with the Employee Compensation Fund (annual return due 31 March; assessment by Commissioner). Domestic minimum wage reportedly N$15.00/hour from 1 Jan 2026 (secondary source, unverified). Households are low-willingness-to-pay buyers; no online filing channel confirmed. Logged as C04.

coverage.category: 2. Scrap-metal dealers
coverage.found: Second Hand Goods Act 23 of 1998 covers scrap metal dealers (certificate, acquisition/disposal registers, copper/brass rules). Police second-hand goods unit said in Oct 2024 it will inspect registers, warn and open cases; many dealers believed non-compliant. Same buyer group and duty as K05 (known).

coverage.category: 3. Second-hand dealers and pawnbrokers
coverage.found: Same Act and police register push as category 2; nothing new beyond K05. Article mentions no electronic record system (only card/online payments advised).

coverage.category: 4. Gold and jewellery buyers
coverage.found: No dedicated gold or jewellery dealer licence found. Diamond Act 13 of 1999 gives Dealer's Licences for rough diamonds (few holders, ministry-issued). Minerals Act s105 permit for high-value minerals possibly applies (not confirmed). Bureau de change (ADLA) regime is tiny (N$1.6m capital). Nothing buildable.

coverage.category: 5. Used car parts and vehicle dismantlers
coverage.found: Search returned no Namibian rules for dismantlers or used-parts dealers (only US/UK/SA material). Not confirmed either way; at most they fall under the Second Hand Goods Act (K05).

coverage.category: 6. Livestock traders, markets and animal transport
coverage.found: Nothing new beyond K06 (NamLITS Online free tool, rejected). Producer/speculator registration under the Meat Industry Act is via Meat Board; see C09 for abattoir/butcher angle.

coverage.category: 7. Small abattoirs and butchers
coverage.found: Abattoirs must be registered/rated under the Meat Industry Act (Meat Board / LLPB, DVS certifies facility); export abattoirs file a self-declaration to the Meat Board; producers must register to market. No butcher/retail-shop licence details found. Few abattoirs; related to K06 buyer world. Logged as C09 (weak).

coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: No search spent; budget used on higher-yield categories.

coverage.category: 9. Veterinary practices and veterinary medicine sellers
coverage.found: Veterinary and Veterinary Para-Professions Act 1 of 2013; regulations GN 17 of 2014 (amended GN 218/2017, 2022 fee amendment) require registration of veterinary practices and para-professional practices, CPD. Small closed group, no recurring report found. Medicine-seller regime not found. Logged as C08 (weak).

coverage.category: 10. Well drillers and water abstraction
coverage.found: Water Resources Management Act 11 of 2013 brought into force 29 Aug 2023 (GN 268/2023) with Regulations GN 269/2023: borehole licences (3-year validity per ministry reply), abstraction licences up to 5 years, licensing of drillers and well constructors. Domestic use outside local authority areas exempt. New regime likely creates backlog of licence applications from farms/lodges/drillers. Logged as C03 (unverified).

coverage.category: 11. Septic, sanitation and waste haulers
coverage.found: No Namibian septic/hauler permit found. Waste activities need MEFT Environmental Clearance Certificate under Environmental Management Act 7 of 2007 (inference only); municipal sewerage by-laws under Local Authorities Act 1992 vary by town. Unverified, nothing concrete.

coverage.category: 12. Lift, boiler and pressure-equipment owners and inspectors
coverage.found: Regulations relating to Health and Safety of Employees at Work (1997, under Labour Act 11 of 2007) require permission to erect/use boilers and elevators, boiler inspection register and log-book, elevator register and record book, periodic examination. Inspector appointment, intervals and penalties not read. Logged as C07 (unverified).

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: No search spent. Only touched via abstraction licences (category 10).

coverage.category: 14. Pesticide and fertiliser dealers and applicators
coverage.found: Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act 1947; Regulations GN 112/2007 amended GN 311/2020: registration of substances, sterilising plants and pest operators with the Registrar; remedy registration valid to 31 March each year. No separate dealer licence or Hazardous Substances licence found. Logged as C10 (weak).

coverage.category: 15. Labour contractors and recruitment agencies
coverage.found: Employment Services Act 8 of 2011 requires licensing of private employment agencies; Labour Act s128 (2012 amendment) makes client the employer of labour-hire workers. On 22 Sep 2026 an MP asked the minister how many agencies are licensed, how many have valid licences, inspections over 3 years, and when an Employment Services Act amendment bill will reach parliament; no answer reported. Logged as C05.

coverage.category: 16. Cemeteries, burial societies and funeral services
coverage.found: No national funeral parlour licensing or undertaker register found. Cemetery rules are municipal (Local Authorities Act 1992 s94; e.g. Oshakati GN 157/2023); Crematorium Ordinance 6 of 1971. Nothing buildable.

coverage.category: 17. Community and religious bodies: associations, charities, halal and kosher supervision
coverage.found: Under the Financial Intelligence Act 2012 and NPO Regulations GN 272/2023 (in force 31 Aug 2023), Directive 4 of 2023: faith-based organisations, religious bodies and charitable NPOs must register with the FIC, update details and file annual returns electronically (2024 returns due 31 Jan 2025); FIC threatens ceasing orders and denial of financial services. Churches report registration done but certification delayed. Corporate Laws Bill 2025 may affect section 21 companies (status unconfirmed). Related to K01 only in regulator, different buyer. Logged as C01. No halal/kosher findings.

coverage.category: 18. Transport operators: minibus, taxi, moto-taxi, small trucking and bus fleets
coverage.found: Road Transportation Act 74 of 1977: public road carrier permits (taxi, passenger, goods) applied through Road Transportation Board, gazetted with 21-day objection window; Roads Authority NaTIS holds files. Current renewal and fleet reporting process not found. Logged as C06 (unverified).

coverage.category: 19. Market traders, street vendors, money changers
coverage.found: Money changers: only Bank of Namibia ADLAs (bureaux de change) may trade; N$1.6m minimum capital, N$5,000 fee; handful of licensees, tiny market. Street vendors and informal trader permits not searched (municipal level).

coverage.category: 20. Small licensed premises with inspections: tattoo studios, driving schools, childminders and nurseries, small food producers, hunting outfitters
coverage.found: Driving schools: Works and Transport proposes 13-point registration (business registration, tax and SSC good standing, Affirmative Action certificate, local authority fitness certificate, insured and dual-control vehicles, registered instructors), regulations expected 1 April 2027 (C02). ECD centres/childminders: Child Care and Protection Act 3 of 2015 and 2019 regulations (GN 6829) require registration, records, staff vetting (C11). Hunting outfitters: NTB registration, professional hunter annual registration, per-client MEFT trophy permits (C12). Tattoo studios and small food producers not searched.

coverage.found: Namibia Tourism Board Act 21 of 2000 plus Registration of Accommodation Establishments Regulations GN 139 of 2004 (guest register and returns). NTB asked unregistered Airbnb-type hosts to register by 30 April 2025 (fine up to N$20,000 or 2 years). Tourism Bill would move regulation to the ministry. Related to K04; see N11.

coverage.category: 30. Small exporters and importers facing traceability or certification rules: food, fish, timber, forest-risk commodities
coverage.found: Livestock and Livestock Products Amendment Act in force 13 Jan 2025: LLPBN permits for exports and imports of poultry, eggs, dairy, hides and skins. Export-approved abattoir, classification and halal rules for meat. Fish: aquaculture export registration, nothing small-exporter-specific. EUDR charcoal is K03. See N01.

coverage.category: 31. Agricultural control boards: LLPBN and Namibian Agronomic Board registrations, permits, levies
coverage.found: New regime from 13 Jan 2025 for poultry, eggs, dairy, hides and skins (producer and facility registration, import or export permits, levy self-declaration, statement by the 7th); NAB controlled crops. See N01 and N02.

coverage.category: 32. Public passenger transport: road carrier permits and taxi registration
coverage.found: Indefinite road carrier permits had to be converted to transitional permits by 30 Sep 2025 ahead of two-year renewable permits; permits applied at any NaTIS office from 1 Feb 2026; ride-hailing must hold public passenger permits; Oshakati taxis must register and mark vehicles by 31 Mar 2027. See N04.

coverage.category: 33. Liquor licensing and shebeens
coverage.found: Liquor Act 1998: annual renewal by 31 March at the magistrate, local-authority fitness certificate required; shebeen crackdowns by municipalities; a Liquor Amendment Bill exists but status unconfirmed. See N05.

coverage.category: 34. Employer statutory contributions and reporting: NTA VET levy, Employment Equity Commission, SSC
coverage.found: NTA VET levy 1% of payroll for payroll of N$1m or more, monthly return by the 20th, N$250 late penalty, Employer Training Grant claim within 31 days of 31 March; Employment Equity Commission affirmative action reports and compliance certificates (valid one year; threshold sources conflict, 10 vs 50 employees); EEC annual reports not published since 2019 and its case management software collapsed. See N08 and N09.

coverage.category: 35. Wildlife, game dealers, taxidermy and hunting outfitters
coverage.found: MEFT registers game dealers (annual renewal) and requires registers and year-end reports; Controlled Wildlife Products and Trade Act 9 of 2008 and Regulations GN 144 of 2011 require registers and returns; trophy hunting operators must register with the NTB and obtain per-client permits. See N06.

coverage.category: 36. Empowerment and local-content verification (NEEEF)
coverage.found: NEEEF is still a bill (no Act found as of late 2025 sources); only buyer-specific rules such as NamPower procurement exist. See N14.

candidates.buyer: Small Namibian contractors, MSMEs and subcontractors bidding on public and parastatal tenders (CIF members, about 430, and non-members)
candidates.category: 27. Construction, mining and quarry contractors and suppliers: site registers, accreditation, local-content reports
candidates.existing: Competitor search (English, 1 query) found no bid-pack or compliance-tracker software for Namibian MSMEs, only the CIF directory and tender notices. This is a thin check; no Afrikaans or Oshiwambo query was run. Generic tender-alert and document-vault tools probably exist (unverified).
candidates.name: Bid-compliance document pack for small Namibian contractors and suppliers (MSME certificate, ownership declaration, tax and social security clearance expiry tracker, tender checklists)
candidates.trigger: Public Procurement Act 15 of 2015 and 2017 Regulations (Annexure 8 on bidder registration); Code of Good Practice on Preferences GN 13 of 2023: a valid MSME certificate, a sworn declaration of at least 51% Namibian ownership, certified IDs, and tax and social security clearance must be current for each bid. Many parastatals (NamPower NEEEP, Namibia Agronomic Board) ask for the same documents.
candidates.unchecked: Whether the buyers pay for it (tender wins are irregular). Whether the tax and social security clearance certificates are issued online and how often. Whether the MSME certificate expires. Whether e-GP or a central supplier portal is planned by the Central Procurement Board. Overlap with generic document-vault ideas.

candidates.buyer: Small sand and gravel contractors and quarries, plus municipalities, town councils and traditional authorities that would issue permits, collect levies and monitor sites
candidates.category: 27. Construction, mining and quarry contractors and suppliers: site registers, accreditation, local-content reports
candidates.existing: Competitor search: no vendor product found in the sand mining results. The EIA consultants (EAPAN members) are the service channel. Local authorities may use their own spreadsheets.
candidates.name: Sand and gravel permit, levy and rehabilitation tracker for small commercial extractors, local authorities and traditional authorities
candidates.trigger: Existing duty: an ECC under the Environmental Management Act 7 of 2007 is required for commercial sand and gravel extraction, and ECCs are time-limited and must be renewed. Draft regulations under the draft Environmental Management Amendment Bill (consulted Jan to Feb 2026) would create three tiers, delegate permits, levies and monitoring to local and traditional authorities, and add rehabilitation and fines.
candidates.trigger_note: Revisit once the regulations are gazetted; if they require permit registers or levy returns, rescore to 4-5.
candidates.unchecked: Draft not final: the text, the comment period, and whether the final rules require registers, returns or levy receipts. The buyer base is unclear: how many commercial operators and how many authorities issue permits. Municipalities buy slowly and there may be public-sector procurement friction. Whether ECC conditions require annual reports (none found).

candidates.buyer: All contractors operating in Namibia (would have to register and be categorised by capacity)
candidates.category: 27. Construction, mining and quarry contractors and suppliers: site registers, accreditation, local-content reports
candidates.existing: None (no regime exists). The CIF runs voluntary registration.
candidates.name: Construction Council contractor registration and categorisation kit (watchlist)
candidates.trigger: Planning and Construction Bill (Namibian Planning and Construction Council): registration with a minimum qualification and bank-balance threshold. Not enacted: the bill stalled at the Cabinet legislation committee as of 2024 and the 2019/20 promulgation target was missed. No 2025 or 2026 update found.
candidates.unchecked: Current bill status in 2025 and 2026 (Parliament, Ministry of Works and Transport, CIF). Not scored higher because there is no duty today.

candidates.buyer: Community water point committees in communal areas (roughly 80% of communal water points have one) and, indirectly, DWSSC regional offices and NamWater
candidates.existing: No tool found. Support is by DWSSC extension officers, who are in short supply.
candidates.name: Water point committee bookkeeping and user-fee remittance app (rural community water points)
candidates.trigger: Water Resources Management Act 11 of 2013 s30 (water point committees), in force since the 2023 notices (GN 268 and 269 of 2023). Committees collect user fees and pay NamWater, and report major repairs to DWSSC.
candidates.unchecked: Whether the user-fee provisions are in force (operative text not seen); whether DWSSC or donors already run a free tool; the buyer is community volunteers with little cash and weak connectivity, so willingness to pay is low and the sale would be to the state or donors. Not a solo-founder-sellable segment unless a donor or DWSSC funds it.

candidates.buyer: Small water services providers: town councils, settlement authorities, lodges and estates, farms and mines that supply water to others
candidates.existing: None found; no competitor search was run because the candidate scores below 3.
candidates.name: Water services provider licence and tariff-filing kit for small private and municipal water suppliers
candidates.trigger: Water Resources Management Act 11 of 2013 s41 (WSP licence), s42 (combined licence), and Regs GN 269/2023 reg 43 (WSP licence application) and reg 2 (tariff norms). The Water Regulator would set tariffs. It was established in 2017 but dormant as of 2021, and operational status in 2025 and 2026 is unconfirmed.
candidates.unchecked: Whether the Regulator is operating, whether licence applications have opened, and how many private WSPs exist. Likely a handful of buyers, mostly municipalities. Rescore if a licensing deadline is announced.

candidates.buyer: Namibian beekeepers (small, members of the Beekeeping Association of Namibia) and pollination hive suppliers
candidates.existing: None.
candidates.name: Beekeeper / apiary register (watchlist, no duty yet)
candidates.trigger: None today. The Animal Health Act 1 of 2011 might be extended to bees and a National Apiculture Framework is under discussion. This would create bee disease surveillance, movement controls and import permits (a 2025 import of bees from South Africa for berry pollination was contested).
candidates.unchecked: Whether any registration or movement permit has been introduced; how many commercial beekeepers exist. Tiny market. Note: K06 (NamLITS) was killed by a free state tool, which suggests a bee register would also be state-run.

coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: No mandatory beekeeper, apiary or hive register exists. Bees are only partly covered by the Forest Act 12 of 2001 (s25) and the Animal Health Act 1 of 2011. A Windhoek stakeholder workshop is feeding a National Apiculture Framework (https://www.namibian.com.na/beekeepers-want-animal-health-act-to-cover-bees/). The Beekeeping Association of Namibia (est. 2021, voluntary, non-statutory) is the only body (https://www.civic264.org.na/environment/beekeeping-association-of-namibia). One 2025 import permit for South African bees for berry pollination drew opposition (https://www.nipdb.com/post/namibia-berries-regulatory-mediation-in-agriculture-the-bee-industry-conflict). No recurring duty found, so no candidate. Revisit only if bees are brought under the Animal Health Act (a hive or apiary register would then be a candidate). Not checked: the Ministry's veterinary services and honey export or food-safety rules.

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: The Water Resources Management Act 11 of 2013 commenced via GN 268/2023, with Regulations GN 269/2023 (dated 29 Aug 2023 per the LAC annotated copy, though one press report says December 2023). It has s30 water point committees, s41 water services provider licensing, s42 combined licence, and reg 43 for WSP licence applications. The regulations include a tariff pricing policy. The Water Regulator was set up in 2017 but dormant as of a 2021 parliamentary reply (https://www.parliament.na/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Response-to-question-by-UDF-Hon-Murorua-on-25-March-2021.pdf). A later press piece shows consultation on establishing it (https://namibian.com.na/?p=822322, undated). I could not confirm that the Regulator is operational or that any licensing window or deadline exists. Rural supply runs on community water point committees that collect user fees and pay NamWater. Committees are weak, and at least half of rural water points are reported faulty. Support sits with the DWSSC government directorate. Candidate: C-NA-W1 below (weak). Unchecked: WSP licensing for lodges, farms, mines and private estates, and whether DWSSC runs a free committee reporting tool.

coverage.category: 27. Construction, mining and quarry contractors and suppliers: site registers, accreditation, local-content reports
coverage.found: (a) No statutory construction council. The Construction Council or Planning and Construction Bill has stalled since the 2010s and was at Cabinet committee stage as of 2024 (https://we.com.na/infrastructure-we/lack-of-construction-law-an-industry-obstacle-cif-warns2024-09-26). Registration is only through the voluntary CIF (about 430 members). (b) Public procurement is where the compliance burden sits. The Public Procurement Act 15 of 2015 and 2017 Regulations (Annexure 8 on bidder registration), plus the Code of Good Practice on Preferences (GN 13 of 2023, in force Jan 2023). Preferences are capped at 10%. MSME bids need an MSME certificate from the trade ministry, a sworn Namibian-ownership declaration with a 51% threshold, certified IDs and tax and social security clearance (https://www.lac.org.na/laws/2023/8020.pdf, https://namqa.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Supply-and-Delivery-of-Branded-Promotional-Items-Lump-Sum-Contract.pdf, https://www.nab.com.na/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/NOTICE-TO-POTENTIAL-BIDDERS.pdf). (c) NEEEF is still unenacted; a World Bank study in 2023 advised against it (https://namibiansun.com/local-news/world-bank-study-says-no-to-neeef2023-05-09). NamPower's NEEEP reserves procurement under N$10m for previously disadvantaged owners (https://neweralive.na/?p=177221). The NEEEP verification mechanics were not verifiable: a search found nothing. (d) Oil and gas: the upstream local content policy requires Local Content Plans in licence applications. Operators and EPCs ask suppliers for registration, certification and insurance. The NIPDB runs supplier sessions (https://www.namibian.com.na/energy-explainer-part-4-govt-must-gazette-local-content-rules/). Local-content rules are not yet gazetted, and the market is a few large suppliers. (e) Sand and gravel: commercial extraction needs an ECC under the Environmental Management Act 7 of 2007. The MEFT warned in Jan 2026 about illegal mining (https://allafrica.com/stories/202601190381.html). Draft regulations were taken to regional consultations from 26 Jan to end Feb 2026. They have three tiers (domestic under 5 m3, domestic over 5 m3 needing approval, commercial with permit and ECC). Local authorities, traditional authorities and landowners would handle permits, monitoring, levies and rehabilitation. This is from a press summary only (https://neweralive.na/?p=375161, https://www.we.com.na/mw-main/curbing-illegal-sand-and-gravel-mining2026-01-16181440). About 900 small-scale mining claims exist under the 1992 Minerals Act. No periodic return forms found for quarry or sand operators. Candidates: C-NA-27a and C-NA-27b (weak), C-NA-27c (watchlist). Unchecked: the draft regulation text, the final 2023 Code definitions of SME, and Annexure 8 forms.

result.competitor: The LLPBN Online Permit System on the LLPBN Portal has been live since 2 Dec 2024 and handles import/export permits, so the permit part is already covered. Registration uses downloadable forms sent by email. Levy returns use a PDF 'return for remittance of levies' plus bank payment. I found no commercial software for LLPBN levy returns or registration.
result.duty: GN 381 of 2024 (Livestock and Livestock Products Regulations, under Act 12 of 1981 as amended), in force from 13 Jan 2025. Poultry, egg, dairy and hides producers, plus importers and exporters, must register as producers (deadline was 15 Mar 2025). Facility operators (poultry abattoirs, egg packing, dairy, tanneries, hide and skin stores) must register separately. Import and export each need a permit. Levy is 0.6% on domestic sales, 0.8% on imports and 1% on live exports. The person responsible must file a statement by the 7th of the following month, even if the levy is already paid, and pay by the end of that month. Failing to register is an offence (we.com.na/PPA). I did not reach the exact penalty amounts or confirm who exactly is the 'person responsible'. The board says the levy is deducted from sale proceeds, which points to buyers and processors rather than small producers. Fetching the regulation text (NamibLII returned 403; LAC PDF/DOCX unreadable) did not work.
result.market: Very small. The Ministry of Agriculture counted 4 dairy farmers in 2022; the Bank of Namibia says fewer than 10 remain. The DVCD programme targets 150 small dairy producers, most of them informal. The Poultry Producers Association has 28 members, and small and medium producers turn out about 60k broilers a week. Industry output was N$1.74bn in 2024. I found no LLPBN count of registered operators. Likely only a few dozen to low hundreds of formal levy filers.
result.reason: The duty is real. GN 381/2024 under Act 12 of 1981 has been in force since 13 Jan 2025. It requires producer and facility registration and import/export permits. Levies are 0.6% on domestic sales and 0.8% on imports. The person responsible must file a monthly statement by the 7th, even if the levy is already paid. Failing to register is an offence. Permits already run on the board's own Online Permit System (since Dec 2024). Levy returns appear to be a PDF form plus bank transfer, and I found no software for them. But the market is tiny: under 10 commercial dairies, 28 PPA poultry members and a few egg packers, tanneries and importers. The levy is deducted at the point of sale, so it falls on buyers and processors rather than smallholders. Willingness to pay is low, so it doesn't work as a standalone product.

Duty is real: FIC requires FBOs, religious bodies and charitable NPOs to register, update details and file annual returns electronically via the FIC portal (Revised Directive 4 of 2023). Sanctions are fines, ceasing orders and denial of banking. The 2024 return was due 31 Jan 2025. No third-party software was found, but the competitor search was shallow (2 searches). The 2025-2026 cycle, NPO count, and portal/goAML details were not verified. Weak commercial case: a small form-filling task done once a year, with a state portal already in place. Buyers are churches and NPOs that are hard to reach and pay little. An MVP could be a checklist or done-for-you service. Narrow and low frequency.

Duty is real: PH/MHG/HG annual MEFT registration, NTB registration for trophy hunting operators, one MEFT permit per client, season 1 Feb to 30 Nov, and export needs a vet certificate plus an MEFT export permit. No software found in two searches. The market is small, with a few hundred operators at most (no register count found). Permits are issued by government, so most paperwork is one-off per client. The core job is mostly document renewal, and NAPHA acts as the guidance and membership channel. Willingness to pay is low and the buyer pool is tiny, though NAPHA could distribute. Competitor and operator-count checks were thin, and I did not verify whether returns are mandatory.

The duty is not yet law. Press reports (Sept 2026) say the Ministry of Works and Transport's 13 requirements are still proposed amendments to the Road Traffic and Transport Regulations 2001. Stakeholder consultations are ongoing, and the planned effective date is 1 April 2027. Nothing is gazetted, so no penalty or frequency can be confirmed. The only recurring element is the annual roadworthiness certificate, and registration looks like a one-off. The number of driving schools was not found. I did not search for competitors. Value is mostly a one-off compliance pack for a small, fragmented market, and the rules could change.

Duty is real: the Water Resources Management Act 11 of 2013 took effect 29 Aug 2023 and requires borehole licences (form WA04) and abstraction licences for commercial, industrial or irrigation use (form WA03). Existing boreholes had to be registered; the window was extended to about 31 Oct 2025 and has now passed. The fee is N$100 per application, and one application can cover several boreholes. I found no online portal, app or competitor, only paper and Excel forms. Weak as a business: the registration was largely one-off, the fee is tiny, licences last 3 to 5 years so renewals are infrequent, and the buyers are scattered farmers who deal through the NAU. Penalty amounts, borehole counts and any metering or returns duty were not verified. Driller licensing is a niche.

Duty is real: Road Transportation Act 1977 permits for taxis and carriers. A 2025 reform replaced indefinite permits with two-year renewable transitional permits, conversion deadline 30 Sep 2025. From 1 Feb 2026 applications go on paper to any NaTIS office. I found no app or portal, so no direct competitor, but I searched only briefly. Weak case: the permit cycle is only every two years, so frequency is low. Buyers are informal, low-margin taxi owners with little willingness to pay. The reform aims to stop permit renting, so a tracker has a thin pain point. Fleet size, market count and penalties not verified. Renewal steps not confirmed.

The duty is real and in force. NAB milling licences are renewed annually, with the 2025/26 deadline of 31 Jan. Renewal needs NamRA and SSC good-standing certificates, a fitness or health certificate, and proof of food-safety compliance. Missing renewal means no operation and no import permits for white maize, wheat or pearl millet. Permits are also withheld while monthly returns or levies are outstanding. I found no miller compliance software. The market is tiny: about 26 registered millers, and Namib Mills holds about 55% of maize and 85% of wheat milling capacity. Too few buyers to support a software product. Not checked: whether returns are filed online, the current levy schedule, Afrikaans and Oshiwambo searches, and the 7th-of-month return date, which I did not see in an opened source.
